title: American Airlines Forecasts Bigger 2026 Loss as Fuel Costs Surge Despite Record Revenue
body:
American Airlines announced on Tuesday that it now expects a larger net loss for 2026, even as the carrier posted a record‑high revenue year. The airline’s outlook was revised downward after the company disclosed that soaring jet‑fuel prices have eroded profit margins and forced a slowdown in capacity expansion plans for the coming year. American becomes the fourth major U.S. carrier to trim its 2026 financial guidance this month, joining United, Delta and Southwest in acknowledging the strain that higher energy costs are placing on the industry.

The carrier reported $53.6 billion in total revenue for 2023, a 13 percent increase over the prior year and the highest figure in its 90‑year history. Yet that top‑line growth was insufficient to offset the impact of fuel, which rose roughly 45 percent on a per‑gallon basis between January 2023 and March 2024. American said fuel accounted for about 30 percent of its operating expenses in the last quarter, up from 24 percent a year earlier. The higher cost base pushed the airline’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) down by nearly $2 billion compared with its previous forecast.

Analysts note that the airline’s decision to curb capacity growth is a strategic response to both cost pressures and demand uncertainty. American plans to add roughly 1.5 million seats in 2024, a modest increase from the 2 million‑plus seats it had targeted before the fuel price shock. By limiting new routes and deferring aircraft deliveries, the carrier hopes to preserve cash flow while it navigates volatile commodity markets. “The airline is essentially choosing to protect its balance sheet rather than chase volume in a price‑sensitive environment,” said Karen Liu, senior aviation analyst at Meridian Research.

The broader industry context underscores the significance of American’s revision. Fuel is the single largest variable cost for airlines, and its price is tied to global oil markets that have been jolted by geopolitical tensions, OPEC production decisions and lingering supply chain bottlenecks. While some carriers have hedged a portion of their fuel exposure, American disclosed that only about 30 percent of its 2024 fuel consumption is hedged, leaving the majority vulnerable to spot‑market fluctuations. United and Delta, which also trimmed forecasts this month, cited similar exposure, suggesting that the current price environment could become a persistent headwind for U.S. airlines throughout the next two years.

Investors reacted cautiously to the news. American’s shares slipped 3.2 percent in after‑hours trading, and the company’s credit rating was reaffirmed but with a “negative outlook” from Moody’s, reflecting concerns about debt servicing capacity under weaker earnings. Nonetheless, the airline’s strong liquidity position—$12 billion in cash and marketable securities—provides a buffer that could mitigate the worst of the financial strain. The carrier also highlighted ongoing cost‑saving initiatives, including workforce optimization, digital ticketing upgrades and renegotiated supplier contracts, which together are projected to shave $500 million off operating expenses by 2025.

Looking ahead, American Airlines’ ability to rebound will hinge on several variables. If global oil prices retreat to pre‑2023 levels, the airline could see a swift improvement in margins and potentially resume a more aggressive growth trajectory. Conversely, sustained high fuel costs could compel further reductions in capacity and perhaps accelerate fleet modernization efforts aimed at fuel‑efficient aircraft such as the Airbus A321neo and Boeing 737 MAX. Market watchers will also monitor consumer demand trends, especially as business travel recovers from pandemic‑induced remote‑work habits. For now, American’s revised outlook serves as a cautionary signal that even record revenue cannot fully insulate legacy carriers from the volatility of energy markets, and the next twelve months will test how effectively the airline can adapt its operations to a higher‑cost environment.
